ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The path network in the attached figure can be regarded as a graph. The top vertex is labeled X, and the lower-right vertex is labeled Y. Denote the unlabeled intersection points as: A = left middle point, B = right middle point, L = lower-left point, C = lower middle point. The nine paths visible in the figure are XA, XB, AB, AL, LC, AC, BC, BY, CY, each 100 m long. Reasoning: The degrees of the vertices are: X is connected to A, B, degree 2; Y is connected to B, C, degree 2; A is connected to X, B, L, C, degree 4; B is connected to X, A, C, Y, degree 4; C is connected to L, A, B, Y, degree 4; L is connected to A, C, degree 2. Therefore all vertex degrees in the entire graph are even. If Ann wants to go from X to Y without repeating any path, the trail formed by the paths she walks must have only X and Y as odd-degree vertices. Since all vertices in the whole graph have even degree, it is impossible to use all 9 edges; some edges must be deleted so that the deleted edges cause a parity change at X and Y. At minimum, one path from X to Y must be deleted; there is no direct XY edge in the figure, and the shortest path from X to Y has 2 edges, for example X-B-Y. Therefore at least 2 fewer edges must be walked, and at most 9 - 2 = 7 edges can be walked. This upper bound can be attained: delete XB and BY, and walk X-A-L-C-A-B-C-Y, using exactly 7 different paths. Therefore the longest route length is 7 × 100 = 700 m.

raw_record.question_text: Each of the nine paths in a park is $100 \mathrm{~m}$ long. Ann wants to go from $X$ to $Y$ without going along any path more than once. What is the length of the longest route she can choose?

method.method_draft: First describe the diagram as a graph: label the unlabeled junctions as A = left middle, B = right middle, L = bottom left, C = bottom middle, with X at the top and Y at the bottom right. Read the nine visible paths as XA, XB, AB, AL, LC, AC, BC, BY, CY. From the image, every vertex has even degree: X and Y each have degree 2, while A, B, C have degree 4 and L has degree 2. Since Ann must start at X and end at Y without repeating an edge, the used edges must form an Euler trail whose only odd-degree vertices are X and Y. Because the full graph has all even degrees, she cannot use all 9 edges; equivalently, the omitted edges must create odd parity at X and Y. The smallest possible omitted set is a path from X to Y, and the shortest such path visible in the diagram has 2 edges, for example X-B-Y. Therefore at least 2 paths must be omitted, so at most 7 paths can be used. Then exhibit that 7 is possible by omitting XB and BY and using the trail X-A-L-C-A-B-C-Y. Since each path is 100 m, the longest route is 7 × 100 = 700 m.
